title: Child stars say fame gives a 'wound' regulation has failed to prevent
text:
At just 16, Hayden Panettiere was handed a pill that would propel her "downfall of addiction".

The US star — who died last week aged 36 — wrote she was given the drug as a teen to boost her energy ahead of a red carpet appearance.

It was just one of the candid disclosures she made in the weeks before her death, in a memoir that laid bare the challenges of child stardom, substance abuse and postpartum depression.

Early coronial reports from Panettiere's death say she suffered a cardiac arrest, while police dispatchers said they were resuscitating the star after a possible "overdose".

The US Drug Enforcement Agency has also reportedly joined the investigation.

And while it's still unknown if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, Panettiere has joined the tragic roll call of former child stars who have died prematurely over the last year or so.

Hayden Panettiere (centre) wrote of how the traumatic storylines she portrayed led her to associate "catastrophe with adoration". (AP: Kevork Djansezian/File)

Her Ice-Princess co-star Michelle Tratchenberg died aged 39 last February, as a result of complications from diabetes — with co-star Rosie O'Donnell later alleging Tratchenberg struggled with addiction before her death.

Daveigh Chase, of The Ring and Lilo & Stitch fame, died in June aged 35 of AIDS, after suffering from drug abuse and homelessness.

Ice Princess director Tim Fywell paid tribute to his dual leads, Hayden Panettiere and Michelle Trachtenberg, saying he would remember them as "two shining talents, gone far too soon". (Getty Images: Alli Harvey/Stuart Weitzman)

Child stars have long been a vital facet of Hollywood, but this latest triad of deaths has reignited calls for better protections.

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar, has joined the calls for better support for child actors. (Reuters: File)

In an essay following Panettiere's death, Even Stevens star Christy Carlson Romano said stars like herself powered "one of the most profitable storytelling machines in the world, while their mental needs are treated as inconvenient or irrelevant".

"Those of us who make it are given the adoration of saints — and then, if we don't climb to A-list fast enough, we're torn down as if we've committed some unspeakable mortal sin. All before our frontal lobes have fully formed," she wrote for Elle.

"Is it any wonder so many of us struggle with addiction?

" The industry gives us the wound and then acts surprised when we reach for something to treat it. "

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar for The Piano, said the deaths were more than coincidence, in a separate statement about Panettiere's death.

"We are not as protected by the 'systems' that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be," she wrote on Instagram.

The first child star who almost lost it all

There is one key piece of US law that enshrines the rights of child stars — and it is nearing 100 years old.

The 1939 Coogan Law is named after Jackie 'The Kid' Coogan, arguably Hollywood's first child star.

At age four, he was foisted onto the screen by Charlie Chaplin to star 1921's The Kid.

Coogan became a hit, making millions but still only received a weekly allowance of $6.25 from his family.

Hours after Coogan (right) filed his lawsuit, the child star act was rushed through legislation. (Wikimedia Commons: Unknown photographer)

Then when he turned 21, he found his mother and manager-turned-stepfather would not give him a cent more.

Coogan eventually won the subsequent lawsuit he waged, albeit recovering only a small portions of his earnings.

As Coogan Law currently stands, it ensures 15 per cent of a child actor's earnings are set aside in a blocked trust, and also codifies issues such as schooling, work hours, and time off.

In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest' The actress, who died on Sunday aged 36, spoke openly about the hardships she experienced throughout her decades in the spotlight.

Yet despite decades of regulation, the extent of Hollywood's alleged 2000s lawlessness has been made fully apparent.

The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

The 2024 documentary Quiet on Set delved into how dialogue coach Brian Peck was brought onto Disney's The Suite Life of Zack & Cody after previous convictions for the sexual abuse of Nickelodeon stars.

Meanwhile, Disney star Alyson Stoner says unsafe working conditions left her malnourished and chronically stressed, despite the labour laws in place.

And just this week, former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau has sued Disney, alleging a middle-aged employee repeatedly raped her on a 2001 set while other visible adults failed to intervene.

These are the same spaces Panettiere grew up in.

And now, some fear a new era of child stars could face similar problems with even less oversight.

Hayden Panettiere said her mother was a "momager" more often than not. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

Fame arrives from 'the first ultrasound'

In 2024, former Disney star Demi Lovato shone a light on a new child star industry, booming and unregulated.

She was ushering in two new Californian bills that brought kidfluencers in line with the financial restraints of Coogan Law.

Risks of promoting children as influencers remain largely unregulated around the world, including in Australia where there is no specific legislation around kidfluencing, despite being a multi-million industry.

Demi Lovato lamented how her young fame had made her the family "breadwinner". (Supplied: Gavin Newsom )

Social media communication researcher Catherine Archer says she has seen how some kids are famous "from the first ultrasound".

What follows can be enormous pressure to gather large followings that may result in thousands of dollars in earnings for the family — with no guardrails.

"If it's your source of income and you're also their parent, there's a bit of a conflict of interest there, isn't it?" Dr Archer notes.

"It's going to be that pressure to continue, particularly if (your child is) getting the likes, the shares and the comments."

Jerome is a four-year-old model who makes thousands. But his fame has a dark side Children are gathering large followings and earning thousands of dollars through social media influencing — but some warn it comes with a dark side.

No case is a better example of the risks of unregulated family vloggers than Utah mother Ruby Franke, who created a "concentration camp-like setting" for two of her four children.

Her daughter Shari Franke later testified to politicians as a "victim of family vlogging".

"If I could go back and do it all again, I'd rather have an empty bank account now and not have my childhood plastered all over the internet," she said.

" No amount of money I received has made what I've experienced worth it. "

Complicating the issue is a general "reluctance to regulate what goes on in people's homes" Dr Archer adds, while acknowledging the entertainment relies on that very access.

"You see the kids in their bathrooms getting ready for bed. You'll see them in their bedrooms getting ready," she says.

"There's this lack of privacy."

Ruby Franke (centre) was arrested after her 12-year-old son escaped through a window, malnourished and badly bruised. (Washington County Attorney's Office via AP)

Saving stars from 'a lawless area'

France now regulates the hours under-16s can work online, their earnings — and their right to be removed from online platforms at their wish.

MP Bruno Studer said the bill was France's duty to protect children from the internet "which must not be a lawless area".

Disturbing rumours have followed Dan Schneider for years. Now people are speaking out The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

Panettiere's death and those of Tratchenberg and Chase have reignited a debate about the treatment of children on movie sets.

Yet the rise of the kidfluencer shows the new and insidious ways child entertainers continue to face harm.

These are children who often just started with a dream to be creative, as Dr Archer says.

"I don't want to say it is 100 per cent all bad because there are things to enjoy," she says.

"But there's definitely another dark side to it too."

As Anna Paquin says, it can be "possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and upsetting stories".

title: Live: Jai Arrow takes the field for emotional ceremonial 99th Souths game
text:
The NRL has bent its rules to allow Jai Arrow to briefly take the field as South Sydney faces his previous club, the Gold Coast Titans.

Arrow, who was forced into retirement after being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, started the game on the field before subbing off for Cameron Murray and will do the same next week to ensure he notches 100 games for the Rabbitohs.

Later, the Roosters and Dolphins meet in a top-four showdown, before the Cowboys try to secure a finals spot with victory over the Tigers.

In the NRLW, the Titans host the Raiders, the Roosters face the Sharks, and the Cowboys take on the Knights.

title: Interest rates, fish and Donald Trump on Icelanders' minds as nation goes to referendum on EU
text:
High interest rates and inflation, a fishing industry under threat and the shadow of Donald Trump are on the minds of Icelanders as the country goes to a referendum this weekend to decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

If this tiny island nation of almost 400,000 people chooses 'yes', they would have a second vote later to seal the deal reached between Reykjavik and Brussels.

Or the people could reject it and keep the status quo.

Iceland's picturesque capital, Reykjavik. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

A Gallup poll this month found voters split on restarting talks with the EU: 46 per cent said they would vote yes and 46 per cent no, with 8 per cent undecided.

Other polls show a majority against actually joining the bloc.

For Icelanders who support the 'yes' side the most compelling argument is around creating economic opportunities and improving cost of living.

Living standards and wages are high, but so are inflation and interest rates.

Economics student Óðinn Freyr Baldursson, 21, is saving up to buy his first home.

Óðinn Freyr Baldursson believes interest rates will eventually go down if Iceland joins the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"The interest rates for mortgages, regular mortgages for homes, are around 9 per cent here in Iceland," Mr Baldursson said.

"Which is more than two times higher than most other places in Europe, and that's the main reason why owning a house here in Iceland is so, so tough."

He said he believed that if Iceland joined the EU and replaced the volatile krona with the euro, interest rates and inflation would come down.

"Just based off of the experience of other countries joining the EU, we can expect that interest rates will decrease by 3 to 4, maybe 5 per cent," he said.

" We need more stability if we want to continue to develop as a country and an economy, and I think the euro is the way to do that. "

The 'no' side fervently disagrees that joining the EU would solve this.

Tourists at Kirkjufellsfoss in Iceland's east. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"Telling people 'we just need to go into the EU because we have so high interest rates, because we have so high inflation' [is wrong], because we have to deal with inflation and the interest rates either way," 'no' campaigner Steinar Ingi Kolbeins, 29, told 7.30.

"For me, that's just that the government is not doing their job."

He said even if Iceland was to have a seat at the table in Brussels, he doubted his country's officials would have much of an impact because it would have fewer seats than the larger nations.

"We have to think about what does the seat at the table look like? What's the size of the chair? And what's the trade-off? What are we letting go of for that seat at the table?" Mr Kolbeins said.

His colleague Magnea Gná Jóhannsdóttir, also 29, said she was motivated to vote 'no' because she wanted "decisions to be made in Iceland by Icelanders".

Steinar Ingi Kolbeins and Magnea Gná Jóhannsdóttir are both planning to vote 'no' in the referendum. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"I don't want to sell the EU the right of our natural resources or fisheries or farming and all the other things that are part of the European Union," she said.

"And [having negotiations] is a not a journey that's free. It costs money. It costs the time of the government."

The government though, argues the time and investment would be worth it and provide more opportunities for the people.

Fears for fishing industry

On the west coast of Iceland, the Snaefellsnes Peninsula is famous for its appearance in the hit TV show Game of Thrones but it is also home to a thriving fishing industry.

Sustainable fishing is central to Iceland's identity and economy — only Icelandic ships can fish within the 200 nautical miles (321 kilometres) of the island and foreign companies can't own fish processing facilities.

Some hope Iceland would get exemptions to protect its fishing industry if it joined the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

If Iceland joins the EU, those in the fishing industry fear the bloc's Common Fisheries Policy will mean these exclusive waters will become a free-for-all.

Arnar Kristjánsson's family business, G.RUN, has been fishing in them for more than 70 years.

G.RUN is the biggest employer in the small town of Grundarfjörður — 80 of the roughly 800 residents work for the company.

Arnar Kristjánsson fears what would happen to Iceland's fishing industry if it joins the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett )

Mr Kristjánsson is firmly against joining the EU.

"The big companies in Europe will swallow up all these small companies and for small towns like this, there will be no more fish production," the third-generation owner said.

"Iceland tries to use our fish stocks in a way that they can keep producing, [but] Europe has not done that. Many of their fish stocks are in a very bad shape and we don't like to have that here."

Sustainable fishing is central to Iceland's identity. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Prominent 'yes' supporter and Reykjavik MP Dagur B Eggertsson said fishing history "matters very much" and Icelandic officials would fight for exemptions so the industry could be protected.

"The kind of detailed plans of how to handle this have been met with the kind of words of flexibility and openness on the EU's behalf," Mr Eggertsson told 7.30.

Reykjavik MP Dagur B Eggertsson supports a 'yes' vote. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"Some people say [exemptions] are out of the question but one of the arguments for a 'yes' in this referendum is exactly to go into negotiations."

Former president of Iceland from 1996 to 2016, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, said he believed exemptions would not happen.

"The core element in the whole EU existence is the commonality of the rules applying to everyone, every country, every economy, so you can't perhaps say, 'Let's try to see what we can get,' no," Mr Grímsson told 7.30.

He said he feared Iceland would be taking a huge step backwards if it was to eventually join the EU.

Former president of Iceland, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, is against joining the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"It took the generation of my parents and grandparents 100 years to gain independence [from Denmark], full control over our powers, the right to negotiate with other countries, to be a sovereign state," the former president said.

" Whatever people say, this is fundamentally about transfer of power [from Iceland] over to EU institutions. "

'No' campaigners see multiple threats

Iceland has been proudly independent since it broke away from Denmark in 1944.

Iceland's referendum will be closely watched by the EU this weekend. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

It first looked at EU entry 17 years ago after the global financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking sector, but walked away after disagreements on several policies, including fishing.

But the world has changed a lot since then.

Iceland sits opposite Greenland, just beside the Arctic Circle, a region the US, Russia and China all want to exploit for resources and new shipping channels as the polar ice melts due to climate change.

US President Donald Trump's ongoing campaign to slap tariffs on allies, and his threats to annex Greenland, before confusing it with Iceland multiple times in a speech at January's Davos Economic Forum, have startled people here.

These developments have prompted some Icelandic policymakers to seek deeper security and economic cooperation with European partners.

A recent poll found the country was evenly divided over whether to rejoin EU talks. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Iceland's already a member of the defence alliance NATO and some European trade agreements, but now the coalition government wants extra reinforcement with EU membership as well.

"I think all countries, especially small and middle sized countries, have to rethink their position and take in how the world has changed," Mr Eggertsson said.

"Wars are not just wars fought with weapons. We also see trade wars going on and threats of tariffs being used. Tariffs are being weaponised.

"So where should we, as Icelanders, seek tighter bonds? I see that within the EU."

The EU will be watching Saturday's referendum closely.

Iceland is famous for its puffins. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Given how peaceful, prosperous and well-positioned Iceland is, this Nordic nation would be seen by many in Brussels as a very good get.

But if the 'yes' vote gets up, the path forward will be tricky — negotiations will require delicate diplomacy and calculated compromise.

For the Icelandic people though, the vote is not about what is in it for the EU, but all about what is in it for them.

title: Tourists having 'dummy spits' in remote WA taking a toll on business owners
text:
West Australian sheep station owner and tourism operator Tim Meecham is used to dummy spits, but not from the flock of 10,000 Damaras he runs in the Gascoyne region.

It's the tourists who complain — about flies, dirt, lack of mobile reception or the sand not being white enough on the 80-kilometre stretch of beach bordering the Indian Ocean.

"I had an old fellow come up to me and he was so angry," Mr Meecham said.

" There was spit coming out of his mouth and he was demanding his money back because we put him down on an ocean view campsite and the waves were too loud. "

Quobba Station has turned some of the outlandish gripes by visitors into parody posts on social media. (Supplied: Quobba Station)

Age of entitlement hits the outback

Nitpicking customers are not new, but there was a time in the outback when it was considered a luxury to have a cold beer, a hot shower and an air-conditioned room.

Isolated communities, roadhouses and tourist camps get food, fuel and furniture trucked in from hundreds of kilometres away and electricity, water, toilets and telecommunications can be fragile systems.

But holiday-makers are demanding more creature comforts.

"There's always 1 per cent of any group of people who're a bit cranky," said Mr Meecham, who has lived on Quobba Station for 50 years.

"But there are more and more people coming, so that 1 per cent is getting bigger."

A busy Mt Barnett Roadhouse in May. It's an essential fuel stop for travellers on the Gibb River Road. (Supplied: Matt Hawke/Downunderlust Photography)

Midway along the Kimberley's famous Gibb River Road, the small number of staff at Mount Barnett Roadhouse might be simultaneously juggling 50 vehicles queuing for fuel and people packed into the general store.

"There's a few dummy spits, absolutely," said co-manager Matt Hawke.

Mr Hawke said he had seen a change in tourists' attitudes in the 10 years since he arrived.

"Every year people get about twice as difficult — a bit more demanding, a bit more in a rush — and this year has been 10 times that," he said.

"There's a lot of people pushing rapid travel, getting the photo and glossing over the realities of living, working and travelling on this road."

Mr Hawke puts part of it down to a reliance on social media for travel advice and expectations at unrealistic levels.

"People are living this for the second time, even though they've never been here before," he said.

"They used to be eyes wide open – 'This is wild!' – and they'd ask us for advice, you'd make friends and it was lovely.

"These days they say, 'I've read this, I've seen this on the internet' and they're telling us how things are."

Locals say many tourists rush to snap Instaworthy photos at places like Galvan's Gorge on the Gibb River Road before dashing to the next place on their list. (ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills)

Mr Meecham agreed that visitors' expectations were fuelled by what they'd seen online.

"There is so much magnificent footage out there that you could almost blame it for a bit of false advertising, because the shots those drones take are just magnificent," he said.

Mr Meecham said many travellers weren't prepared for basic or isolated camping conditions.

" There's people leaving the city that are just so far disconnected from rural or outback Australia that when they turn up out here … they're actually put into shock. They get angry. "

A chalkboard outside Mount Barnett reminds people to stay nice. (Supplied: Matt Hawke)

Mr Hawke has also noticed a decline in courtesy from holiday-makers.

This included ignoring bush traditions like leaving gates as you find them, helping stranded motorists or being able to change their own tyres.

"People have taken a lot of liberties with other people's safety with speed, not concentrating behind the wheel or barrelling through blind with no lights in the dust," he said.

Bad influencers lead travellers astray

Mr Hawke's other concern is social media travel posts — both human and AI-generated — containing out of date or factually incorrect information.

"No-one’s fact-checking them … it's potentially ruining people's trips," he said.

"I think it's really starting to frustrate local operators and, I imagine, in other areas in Australia, with the inaccuracies."

Mr Hawke recommended holiday-makers speak directly to local tourist bureaux, tour operators or businesses and residents.

An AI-generated social media post details fuel stops on the Gibb River Road. The information and image contain several errors. (ABC Kimberley)

Mr Meecham said most Quobba visitors were "gobsmacked by the scenery" and appreciated its remoteness

"It is just a small per cent of people that just aren't suited for this kind of holidaying," he said.

"I would far rather have to deal with a mob of cranky ewes, trying to put them through a gate for half a day, than dealing with a cranky tourist.

"The ewes are so much easier to deal with."

title: Trump says US is taking partial control of Venezuela's oil reserves
text:
US President Donald Trump says the US has entered an agreement with Venezuela to take control of a fifth of the South American country's vast oil reserves.

Mr Trump announced the deal in a social media post on Friday, local time, providing few details about it other than that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.

"The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Mr Trump wrote.

Donald Trump said the "historic" transaction would lower gas prices in the US. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

"At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer."

Ms Rodríguez's government in a statement said the deal involved the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels.

It said the agreement could draw $US100 billion ($139b) in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $US209 billion ($291b) in taxes for Caracas.

Ms Rodríguez in a posting on Telegram predicted the deal "will have a significant impact on our nation's revival".

Delcy Rodríguez opened Venezuela's oil sector to privatisation shortly after taking power this year. (Reuters: Leonardo Fernandez Viloria)

The agreement allows for the United States to partner with an unnamed private operator in Venezuela to create a new private company to take hold of the reserves, according to a US official familiar with the contours of the deal.

The official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that Ms Rodríguez granted the company 100-year rights to develop the oil fields.

The deal gives the United States 55 per cent effective output of the new private company — including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost.

The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.

The announcement comes nearly nine months after the US military at Mr Trump's direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's president Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

Trump under pressure to lower oil costs

Mr Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran reaches a six-month mark with no conclusion in sight.

The US has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

The US-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20 per cent of the world petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

The average price of gas in the US stood at about $4.09 a gallon ($1.51/litre) on Friday, according to the American Automobile Association. The average price was $3.21 ($1.18/litre) at the same time last year.

A significant drop in US gas prices tied to the agreement is not expected immediately.

Experts have repeatedly warned that a substantial boost in Venezuelan oil production will not happen quickly as repairing and expanding infrastructure takes years and requires billions of dollars.

Persuading big American oil companies to return to the region could face headwinds given the unrest and decades of badly damaged infrastructure.

Days after the ouster of Mr Maduro, Mr Trump gathered oil executives at the White House and called on them to rush back into Venezuela. Executives expressed interest in the opportunity but there was also a measure of caution given their past experience in the country.

How the Trump administration runs Venezuela and takes its money Amid the fallout of devastating twin earthquakes Donald Trump says the US has been taking "billions and billions of dollars from Venezuela". So who is running the country and what is happening with the seized funds?

Darren Woods, CEO of ExxonMobil, the largest US oil company, said at that moment he saw the country as "un-investable".

But Mr Trump has insisted that his administration has brought a measure of stability to Venezuela.

He has argued that Venezuela stole US oil when former Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez moved decades ago to nationalise hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.

Ms Rodriguez, in one of her early moves after taking power, signed a law that opens the nation's oil sector to privatisation and reversed a bedrock tenet of the self-proclaimed socialist movement that had ruled the country for more than two decades.

Mr Rubio said on X that the agreement would usher in $US100 billion ($139b) in private investment into Venezuela and lead to lower gas prices in the United States.

"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," Mr Rubio posted.

The oil bought from the new company would go toward filling the US strategic petroleum reserve and toward military use, according to the US official.

Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground — about 17 per cent of the world's supply, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela's soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1 per cent of the world's oil.

Mr Maduro remains jailed in the US. He has pleaded not guilty.

AP/Reuters

title: Magpies legend Pendlebury set to join Gold Coast Suns for 2027 season
text:
Collingwood legend and AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury will move to the Gold Coast Suns in 2027.

Pendlebury, who has played 442 games for the Magpies, will move to the Suns as an unrestricted free agent.

The contract is believed to be a multi-year agreement, where the 38-year-old will play a hybrid coaching and on-field role for two seasons, before moving into an assistant coach role for another two years.

Pendlebury was not offered a new contract to continue his career at Collingwood.

"For the past 21 years, it's been an incredible privilege to be a Collingwood footballer. From walking in the doors as a 17-year-old, to seeing the way everyone at the club has welcomed and embraced my family over all these years is something that is truly special," Pendlebury said in a statement.

"I've spent the majority of my life here and so many of my best memories have come through being part of Collingwood. The friendships, the challenges, the successes and even the tough times have all shaped who I am.

"The privilege of pulling on the Collingwood jumper has never been lost on me. I understand what this club means to so many people and I've always tried to represent it in a way that makes our Magpie Army proud.

"This decision has not come lightly but I know this is the best thing for me and my family as I transition into the next phase of my football journey."

The midfielder will leave the Magpies as one of the club's greatest-ever players, having won two premierships, a Norm Smith medal and six All-Australian nods.

His role at the Suns is set to mimic former Hawthorn legend Luke Hodge's 2018 move to the Brisbane Lions, where Hodge played two seasons as an on-field coach for a young Lions squad that has gone on to win two premierships from three grand final appearances.

The deal will be officially ticked off when the AFL's free agency period begins on October 2.

Pendlebury was denied a finals farewell game in Collingwood's wildcard loss to the Western Bulldogs on Friday night after straining his hamstring in the final game of the regular season.

title: 'Once-in-a-lifetime' mourning ceremony for Bendigo's Russell Jack
text:
A state funeral unlike any other has been held in regional Victoria today to honour a long-serving leader of Bendigo's Chinese community.

Russell Jack was farewelled in a traditional Cantonese mourning lion ceremony, believed to be the first in living memory for the region.

A state funeral is being held in Bendigo today for Russell Jack AM. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll did not attend today's state funeral, but instead announced this morning that he was forming an independent, bipartisan panel to review how Victoria commemorated officials with state services and statues.

Former premiers Jacinta Allan and John Brumby were in attendance.

In her tribute at the funeral, Ms Allan described Mr Jack as "one of Bendigo and Victoria's greatest".

She said Mr Jack was a "proud Chinese Australian" who shared his culture "generously"

At the conclusion of Russell Jack's funeral the white mourning lion will be burned along with traditional paper offerings. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

"Russell was such a proud Chinese Australian. He lived and breathed his culture and also, too, so significantly, he shared it generously," Ms Allan said.

" And it is thanks to Russell that right here in Bendigo we are home to a living record of the contribution Chinese Australians have made to Bendigo but also too, to our nation. "

Jacinta Allan spoke at the state funeral of Russell Jack in Bendigo on Saturday. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Ms Allan said Mr Jack had "ensured that the story of the Chinese migrants who came here to the goldfields of Central Victoria in the 1850s but who then stayed, worked hard and raised their families here would be honoured, would be remembered and would be celebrated."

Anita Jack said her father's legacy, beyond the institutions he built and heritage he preserved, was the "lives quietly altered".

"To dad it was simply taking interest in a young person who at that moment needed someone to see something worthwhile in them," she said.

"We are immensely proud of him and know how extraordinarily lucky we are."

Russell Jack's daughter Anita, with her daughters Stellina and Amelita Baxter, walks behind the hearse at today's state funeral in Bendigo. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

Richard Louey, a longtime participant in the dragon team at the annual Bendigo Easter parade, also said Mr Jack's care for children in need was "his single most important legacy".

Mr Jack led the Bendigo Chinese Association for more than 30 years, established the Golden Dragon Museum and was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia for service to the preservation of Bendigo's Chinese heritage and culture.

Russell Jack "devoted his life to ensuring that Bendigo's Chinese traditions did not disappear", his family said. (Supplied: The Jack family)

The traditional Cantonese white mourning lion is distinct from the bold, bright colours seen at celebrations like the annual Bendigo Easter Parade.

Two members of Bendigo's lion team have been chosen to perform the white lion, with six others who will play a low, sombre beat on instruments.

"It's a once-in-a-lifetime occasion for some members of our lion team," Bendigo Chinese Association president Doug Lougoon said.

The mourning lion was made especially for the occasion in Hong Kong, by the same maker of Bendigo's newest, 125-metre dragon Dai Gum Loong.

"There's a real great connection between the family and the dragon maker Master Hui," Mr Lougoon said.

The lion accompanied Mr Jack and his family through Bendigo's Dai Gum San Chinese precinct, and on to the state funeral service at Ulumbarra Theatre.

Russell Jack with Prince Charles and Princess Diana in Bendigo in 1983. (ABC News)

At Bendigo Cemetery the elaborate display of Chinese culture ended with the ceremonial burning of the mourning lion and firecracker.

Each guest was given an offering, a small coin and a lolly to remove any "bitterness" before they returned home.

title: Street artists turn rusting opal machinery into outback spectacle
text:
The vast flat plains of outback NSW are not normally associated with the explosive visuals of street art covering Melbourne's laneways.

But acclaimed artist John Murray's love of both places plans to change that.

He has started turning discarded mining equipment in a remote north-west NSW town into a canvas for street artists from across the country.

Oli Ruskidd's art was inspired by the iridescent colours of opals that Lightning Ridge is famous for. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

Known for his own colourful murals across regional New South Wales and Queensland, Murray invited street artists to Lightning Ridge to paint old "agitators" — the mixing drums once used by miners to sift soil in the search for opals.

"It's mainly set up just to promote street art," Murray said.

" I've met all these awesome artists in the street art scene and want to bring them to Lightning Ridge. "

John Murray's iconic emu motif graces one side of a discarded agitator … (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

… while his wife and fellow artist Viki painted the other in a nod to local wildlife. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

From mines to masterpiece

The agitators-cum-canvases were all donated for the project, Murray said.

The retired drum mixers are scattered around Lightning Ridge, mostly scrapped or left to rust in paddocks.

"The agitators are all old, abandoned mixers from the opal mines," Murray said.

Visiting artists are given a blank canvas to work with as part of John Murray's art agitator project. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

Unlike most public art projects, the artists were not given a brief, and there was no committee sign-off.

"There are no gatekeepers on the project, so they can paint whatever they want," Murray said.

"It's an opportunity to do free-form street art."

So far, six of a planned 20 agitators have been painted by artists Manda Lane, Joanne Travis (N2O), James Wilson, Lukas Kasper, Oli Ruskid, and John and his wife Viki, a fellow artist.

Murray said a goal was to host a 50/50 split of women and men to support the growing cohort of female street artists.

John Murray wanted to give artists the opportunity to paint whatever they liked. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

"The women are awesome," he said.

"It used to be such a male-dominated field, and it's great to see more women coming through."

He and Viki have self-funded the effort, with his estimated final cost expected to be around $150,000.

Visiting artists are covered for around four nights' accommodation, meals, and $500 towards fuel costs.

They are also shown around the town and given some materials like the base coat and finish for their agitator.

Yabbies and the bright outback night sky feature on Lukas Kasper's agitator in Lightning Ridge. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

Yabbies under a night sky

An artist who had already made the trip was Melbourne-based Lukas Kasper, who met Murray in 2019 and had been inspired by his work.

Lukas Kasper has previously collaborated with John Murray on a water tower in Bourke. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

"[John] came down many years ago now and wanted to paint in the laneways," the 32-year-old said.

"We painted heaps all through the city, all through Melbourne, and he basically became one of my best mates."

The pair have painted together several times, including working on a water tower in the nearby town of Bourke where Kasper assisted Murray with two other artists, Bob Barrett and Brian Smith.

"So when he pitched the idea of coming back, I couldn't get there quick enough," he said.

For his agitator, Kasper drew inspiration from a mural he had just finished in the western NSW town of Coonamble, where he had painted a series of yabbies.

Lukas Kasper painted a toilet block in Coonamble, south of Lightning Ridge, with a team of local artists. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

The other side of the toilet block in Coonamble. (Supplied: Lukas Kasper)

Murray told him local kids in Lightning Ridge often went yabbying in local dams and waterways.

"There's that little connection to the local space," Kasper said.

His finished design added a "galactic" flair, with a star-studded sky across the top — a nod to the outback sky he said he rarely got to see from Melbourne.

Lukas Kasper travelled from Melbourne to Lightning Ridge as part of the art agitators project funded by John Murray. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

An open-air outback gallery

When finished, Murray envisioned the painted drums would be arranged as an open-air gallery in the region's renowned Three Mile opal field alongside the Opal Miners Hall of Fame.

Murray said visitors would be able to scan a QR code on each "agi" to learn about who donated the agitator and the artist who painted it.

"Nowhere else in the world would be able to do something like this," he said.

"There's just not that many agitators anywhere else in the world that could be given to something like this."

Artists are supported to come to Lightning Ridge by local artist John Murray to paint old mining agitators. (Supplied: WorksByNathan)

title: Push to declare garden favourite sold at Bunnings a weed
text:
These pretty, purple flowers with a deceptively pleasant name are becoming a problem in Australia.

Polygala, sold under innocent-sounding labels as "sweet pea", "Bellerine pea" and "parrot bush", is overtaking large tracts of Australia's coastline.

That has prompted the Invasive Species Council to nominate Polygala myrtifolia (also known as myrtle-leaf milkwort) as one of Australia's most significant weeds, even as potted examples continue to line shelves in retail stores.

Polygala is routinely sold at Bunnings and other retail chains.

Rows of potted milkwort, also known as polygala or "sweet pea", on sale at Bunnings. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said the thick shrub, originally from southern Africa, had colonised the south-eastern Australian coastline at the expense of native flora.

"It just takes over," Dr Booth explained.

" It forms a dense shrub layer which excludes native plants, mainly on and near the coast, but it also transforms the habitat and, through that, deprives native wildlife of important resources. "

Dr Carol Booth. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

The Invasive Species Council targeted Bunnings last year for stocking gazania seeds.

Gazania, banned in South Australia and recognised as an environmental weed in Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland, and New South Wales, is still permitted to be sold in most states.

ABC News found packets of gazania in a Victorian store when it discovered the rows of potted polygala.

Bunnings has confirmed Polygala myrtifolia and its hybrids are sold through nurseries and plant retailers across Australia but that it focused on selling hybrid polygala, which differs from Polygala myrtifolia.

The hardware and gardening retailer said it would continue to monitor invasive weed regulations, update its products accordingly and customers should read plant label descriptions before buying.

Gazania seeds for sale at Bunnings. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

A growing problem

Australia has a government-endorsed list of 32 Weeds of National Significance (WONS), which threaten the nation's agriculture and environment.

Dr Booth said the list needed updating to include milkwort and other plant varieties that threaten Australia's biodiversity.

At the very least, milkwort should be added to a list of plants banned for sale in Australia, she said.

"Unfortunately, this is fairly typical in Australia. Plant regulation in Australia is a complete mess," Dr Booth said.

"It's not aligned with risk, it's not focused on preventing most invasions and it's not in the public interest," she said.

Polygala is native to South Africa. (Supplied: Biosecurity SA)

The Invasive Species Council estimates about 3,000 introduced plant species have naturalised in Australia.

That means about one in nine species growing in the wild is not native to that area.

More than 1,000 are considered invasive, which means they cause harm to native species and ecosystems.

"Australia's got a huge weed problem. It's our most expensive land management problem, our most expensive nature conservation problem," Dr Booth said.

"Most plants that can cause harm out in the wild are still available for sale.

" It's leaving future generations an immense burden because a lot of plants still have a long way to spread. "

We will fight them on the beaches

The characteristics that make polygala popular with suburban gardeners as a ground-covering shrub – hardiness and an ability to survive and thrive in dunes, rocky outcrops, and other marginal environments – also ensure it is especially difficult to remove once established.

Volunteer groups, including Nepean Peninsula Landcare, are on the front line of efforts to control the invasive bush, and say it is an uphill battle.

Removing Polygala along the coastline is labour-intensive prompting calls for a biological solution. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

"If you come down to the Mornington Peninsula, you can't miss it. You don't have to look for it, it's everywhere," Nepean Peninsula Landcare volunteer John Dewhurst said.

"It is the most dominant plant through the coastal dune systems and all along the foreshore.

" When it gets an opportunity to thrive, it takes over the whole zone that it occupies. We call it 'the beast.' "

Polygala is found along Australia's southern coastline, from Western Australia through South Australia, Victoria and the New South Wales coast.

There are two ways to remove the weed, but each has its drawbacks.

Herbicides may be effective but are expensive and have the potential to damage native flora.

The most practical way to deal with milkwort is to remove it manually, which is time-consuming and exhausting for the volunteers.

Landcare volunteers manually removing milkwort along the southern Victorian coastline. (Supplied: Nepean Peninsula Landcare)

That's prompted Nepean Peninsula Landcare and the Invasive Species Council to investigate a potential biological control.

"We have engaged some expert scientists, both in Australia and South Africa, to try to find a biocontrol for Polygala," Mr Dewhurst said.

Nepean Peninsula Landcare volunteer John Dewhurst. (Supplied: Nepean Peninsula Landcare)

"It's called 'the Poly Gone project' and that involves locating insects or fungus in South Africa where it comes from that control it naturally.

"Whenever you mention the word 'biocontrol', people think cane toad, but there've been many, many successful biocontrols introduced into Australia, like the prickly pear moth.

"The research is being done in South Africa to ensure it's safe before something happens here."

More weeds of national significance

In 1999, Australia's federal and state governments nominated their original 20 weeds of national significance (WONS) that represented the greatest threat to Australian agriculture and the environment.

A further 12 were added in 2012.

Flowering Gazania (Gazania rigens) plants. (Supplied: Andrew Mitchell, Centre for Invasive Species Solutions)

The National Biosecurity Committee, made up of Australian Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry representatives, plus others from each state and territory government, was in the process of adding new weeds to the WONS list, said Dr Booth.

Those prioritised as potential weeds of national significance include:

African lovegrass (Eragrostis curvula)

European olive (Olea europaea)

Amazon frogbit (Limnobium laevigatum)

Ox-eye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare)

Arum lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica)

Sea spurge (Euphorbia paralias)

Calotrope (rubber bush) (Calotropis procera)

Siam weed (Chromolaena odorata)

Giant rat's tail grass (Sporobolus pyramidalis)

Spanish heath (Erica lusitanica)

Harrisia (Harrisia martinii)

Tropical soda apple (Solanum viarum)

Neem tree (Azadirachta indica)

Wandering trad (Tradescantia fluminensis)

"The list will grow but it's only a very small proportion of the weeds that really are nationally significant, so it's ultimately the ones which state and territory governments agree to put some money into coordinating control," Dr Booth said.

"Unfortunately, we have got so many more than this small list of species that really warrant substantial control," he said.

title: Council plans $15-25m bus stop upgrade amid anti-social behaviour concerns
text:
Massage shop manager Jim Ji says the sound of rowdy bus passengers is terrible for his business.

He said customers at Tai-Chi Traditional Massage in Launceston often arrived "hoping to fall asleep" and tended not to return if outside noise was too distracting.

Jim Ji is concerned about behaviour in the Launceston CBD. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He is among many business owners on St John Street who have long been concerned that nearby bus stops are a lightning rod for antisocial behaviour, particularly among young, school-aged people.

Capri Launceston director Heidi Ellen said she shut the doors twice in a week recently because staff felt uncomfortable about behaviour outside.

"We definitely have customers talking about how they're afraid to come into our store, especially from about 2pm onwards," she said.

"It's getting out of hand."

Could new 'Step + Ride' be the solution?

The Launceston City Council recently advertised a design services tender for a "nation-first Step + Ride" to replace the current bus interchange, with an "indicative" construction budget of $15-25 million.

The Launceston City Council is considering a project that could cost $15-$25 million to upgrade these bus stops. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

It is the latest in a long line of plans designed to address issues at the bus stop, which some local business owners said were persisting, even though security guards had been employed to patrol the area since March.

Mayor Matthew Garwood said the aim was to "create a transport hub that works for the way people move around the city now and into the future".

When asked what would make it a "nation-first" project, a council spokesperson said it was "not aware of another facility described as a step and ride interchange facility".

Tender documents show council envisages a hub where commuters can park bikes and scooters or get lifts through ride-share apps, as well as catch buses.

The Launceston City Council is paying security guards to patrol the St John St bus interchange. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"Stepping as a movement can relate to walking or stepping on and off a bus," it states.

"While 'ride' is a term that can mean riding a bus, riding a bike or ride-sharing."

The chosen designer will be asked to design two potential "Step + Ride" locations — either keeping the bus stops where they are, or moving some of them two blocks north.

The Launceston City Council is currently considering only minor changes to the bus interchange. (Supplied: Launceston City Council)

Council is expected to vote on the exact location in October.

The tender brief states "the project will deliver safer, more attractive, and people-focused bus facilities", which will improve safety through "clear sightlines, passive surveillance and strong day and night presence".

Doubts over plan

Businesses frustrated over the anti-social behaviour doubt whether the planned bus stop redevelopment is the answer.

"I don't think we should spend $15 million or $25 million on that because that's too much," Mr Ji said.

The St John St bus interchange has long been blamed for antisocial behaviour. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Launceston City Councillor Tim Walker also questioned the price tag.

"It was a shock to me when it was pointed out in the tender documents that $15 to $25 million was the price range that we're talking about," he said.

Tim Walker worries antisocial behaviour will persist following the planned bus stop redevelopment. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Asked whether the state government should contribute to the project, a Launceston City Council spokesperson said that was up to them but noted bus interchange funding committed at the 2024 state election never eventuated.

"City of Launceston was disappointed that the state committed $12 million at the state election but then later reneged on this promise," a spokesperson said.

A state government spokesperson said this funding commitment was contingent on the bus stop being relocated to Paterson Street, but that project fell over.

They said it remains committed to working with the council on its revised plan for Launceston interchange.

Cr Walker also questioned whether millions would be spent upgrading the stops, only to have the issues persist.

"Antisocial behaviour, whether it's at bus stops or anywhere else, is an issue that needs to be addressed as a whole of community," he said.

" The bus stops are not going to address that — moving them, changing them, it's not going to make a difference. "

Call for broader strategies

Data from Tasmania Police showed total criminal offences in Launceston were down last financial year, compared to the year before.

It also showed offending among 10 to 17-year-olds had reduced, with 230 total offences last year in that cohort, compared to 337 the year prior.

The age group with the highest level of offending was consistently 25 to 34-year-olds.

The Launceston City Council has commissioned multiple reports which advised leaving the bus stop where it is. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"Police will continue to work closely with council, local businesses and the broader community to identify appropriate pathways for early intervention and remain proactive in their visibility and interdiction with recidivist offenders," he said.

Vicky Nagy, a senior lecturer in criminology at the University of Tasmania (UTAS), said young people were often blamed for issues because they were highly visible, due to being loud or wearing school uniforms, when they were not doing anything wrong.

But she said if antisocial behaviour was an issue, a broader approach was likely needed.

"Improving sight lines and redesigns of things like bus shelters and where stops are can be beneficial because people feel safer in that sort of area," she said.

" But again, it doesn't actually deal with the issues that underlie it, which are oftentimes social issues. "

Michael Guerzoni, another senior lecturer in criminology at UTAS, agreed focusing on the root causes underlying antisocial behaviour was critical.

Michael Guerzoni says authorities should focus on underlying causes for antisocial behaviour. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Dr Guerzoni said the focus should be whether there were youth centres where young people could meet friends, if there were enough supports for families or opportunities for young people without "being under constant surveillance".

Mr Ji, meanwhile, suggested there were other ways council could support local businesses, suggesting a program to attract new operators, rebates for customers or a reduction in parking fees.

title: Melbourne council ditches e-bike and e-scooter trial amid complaints
text:
An inner-Melbourne council has voted to scrap a trial of shared e-bikes and e-scooters, marking the end of shared e-scooters north of the Yarra River.

Darebin councillors voted to scrap the trial, which had been running for six months in the municipality's southern suburbs of Northcote, Fairfield and Alphington.

Council officers found there had been 14,725 trips over the six months, an average of 98 trips a day, travelling an average 2.15 kilometres.

But Mayor Emily Dimitriadis told a council meeting that 93 per cent of feedback was negative.

"Throughout the trial, residents continued reporting e-scooters and e-bikes blocking footpaths, parked incorrectly and creating accessibility issues, riders with no helmets, e-scooters and e-bikes travelling on footpaths," she said.

Emily Dimitriadis says the community has rejected the scheme. (Instagram: Emily Dimitriadis)

Officers found most people who used the trial used it to connect to public transport, and that usage peaked overnight.

But parking the bikes and scooters was a problem when officers inspected 279 allocated parking bays.

"Untidy parking including non-compliant, toppled or misplaced devices was observed at 30 per cent of all bays," a council report presented at the meeting said.

Cr Dimitriadis said the scheme also went over budget, despite the operator, Lime, paying Darebin $18,000.

"Council not only spent $50,000 to set up the trial, it also spent more money administering and managing the trial," she said.

Residents had raised issues with e-bikes and e-scooters being left in the middle of footpaths. (Supplied: Matthew Zammit)

Environmental and transport benefits argued

Darebin resident Matthew Zammitt organised a petition against the scheme, which attracted 1,227 signatures.

He told the meeting he had had trouble negotiating around abandoned e-bikes with a pram, with bikes blocking footpaths, driveways and entrances to train stations.

"It's the modern-day monorail," he said, referencing an episode of The Simpsons where the city invests in a transport scheme that ultimately fails.

" Councils are being duped into thinking that this solves transport woes. "

In an episode of The Simpsons, the townspeople are convinced to spend millions of dollars on a monorail rather than fixing Main Street. (Supplied: 20th Century Fox)

But former Darebin mayor Suzanne Newton, who brought the initial scheme to Darebin, told the meeting the scheme had many benefits for the climate and getting people out of cars.

"Particularly for the so-called last mile journey, to get people home from the train or tram or bus," she said.

She said there was some "pushback", but the trial also showed benefits, including nearly half of trips started or ended at a public transport stop, and 37 per cent were said to replace a car journey.

Councillor Ruth Jelley called on the council to continue the trial, arguing the climate benefits should not be overlooked — council officers found riders saved approximately 1.16 tonnes of carbon emissions.

"How can we call ourselves climate leaders if we fail to deliver on key actions in our climate emergency plan?" she said.

"We are now falling behind NSW and other cities around the world in supporting micromobility through shared schemes such as this.

"Short-termism is killing our climate leadership ambitions, and it's also killing our planet."

Ninety-three per cent of feedback council received about e-bikes and e-scooters was negative. (Supplied: Matthew Zammit)

In July, Yarra council ended a six-year shared e-bike scheme with Lime, saying the operator refused to take responsibility for dumped bikes.

The City of Melbourne dumped its e-scooter scheme in 2024, although there are 500 shared e-bikes available in the city through Lime.

Across the river, in Port Philip, Lime and Neuron operate shared e-scooter schemes, with more than 1.5 million trips since 2022, according to the council, while bayside Frankston, south of Melbourne, ended its micromobility trial in 2024.

In December 2025, the regional city of Ballarat voted to continue its shared e-bike and e-scooter service.

Lime said in a statement that Darebin's decision to end the trial was "not a failure of the council's judgement, but geography".

"When the City of Yarra ended its e-bike scheme in July, the corridor between Darebin and the city closed, and Darebin was left with a network that couldn't go anywhere," said Lime's head of Asia-Pacific, Will Peters.

"This is the result when a network service is regulated on a municipality-by-municipality basis."

He agreed with council that "shared micromobility is public transport, and public transport is the state's domain."

"Darebin's trial produced real evidence, and council is right to take it into its Integrated Transport Strategy," Mr Peters said.

"It belongs in a state conversation about how shared transport is governed in Victoria.

"We'll keep working with councils and the Victorian government to get there."

title: The Gold Coast moment that crystallised Scott Pendlebury’s move
text:

Scott Pendlebury’s ambitions to become a senior coach were crystallised two months ago while the Collingwood great was sitting in the box with Craig McRae coaching against what would become his new club Gold Coast. Pendlebury has donned the black and white for the final time and will play out his career as a Sun as part of a transition into a coaching career. Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury will join Gold Coast next year. Joe Armao The league’s games record holder has decided to accept a four-year contract from the Suns, which will include two years as a player and two as a coach. There are options for that deal to be modified if Pendlebury cannot see out the term on the field. He will be 40 by the end of the two-year playing contract. Pendlebury’s management and Collingwood chief Craig Kelly are in discussions for the dual premiership player and five-time Copeland Trophy winner to be paraded at a Pies home game early next season at a time that also suits his new club. The Pies will also pay tribute to him at their best-and-fairest function.

“There’s plans in place for Collingwood to celebrate Scott’s amazing career at the Collingwood Football Club,” said Pendlebury’s manager Anthony Panozzo, of Hemisphere Sports. Pendlebury’s decision to move to the Suns is a fillip for the expansion club, which failed to live up to lofty expectations this season. Loading The Suns, who finished 13th, beat Essendon to win the services for Pendlebury, who knocked back a more lucrative offer from the Bombers to wear the red and black. According to a well-placed industry source with knowledge of the matter, Pendlebury felt he could provide the Suns’ talented young list with direction on and off the field.

The move allows Pendlebury to cut his teeth as a coach under triple premiership mentor Damien Hardwick and experience life at another club after 21 seasons and 442 games at Collingwood.

Though Pendlebury had been linked to the Suns, as reported previously by this masthead, news of his departure capped off a whirlwind 12 hours for the Magpies, who bowed out of the premiership race in heartbreaking fashion on Friday night in what proved to be Steele Sidebottom’s 375th and final game. Pendlebury refused to go into depth about the move but both player and club said the parting was amicable. “This is a career opportunity for me that’s going to progress me to the next level I want to get to,” Pendlebury said at a press conference on Saturday at the Pies’ headquarters, with the club’s 16 premiership cups as a backdrop. “We’re all very aligned.” Loading Pendlebury is widely considered to be a coach in waiting, but he said there was a period when he was unsure if he would pursue that path.

“I’ve got ambitions to be a senior coach, definitely, and that was part of the discussions we had as well,” Pendlebury said. “I think for a little bit of time there, I probably wasn’t sure what I wanted to do, but I remember sitting up there on the Gold Coast this year and actually coaching with ‘Fly’, and the passion that gave me then, that’s part of the decision-making here, too. It’s the career opportunity that I’ve got. That’s definitely an ambition of mine.” The timing of Pendlebury’s announcement meant Magpies fans were denied the chance to send him off. Steele Sidebottom and Scott Pendlebury’s Collingwood careers are over. AFL Photos Pendlebury declined the opportunity to farewell supporters after the wildcard final defeat, preferring instead to stand in a guard of honour for Sidebottom, so his great friend could have the moment to himself.

“That was beautiful, and I didn’t want to distract from that at all,” Pendlebury, who felt the love of the fans in his record-breaking game in May, said. Related Article AFL 2026 Bulldogs v Magpies player ratings: The crucial moments and costly errors that decided the first wildcard final “Me and my family have had an amazing 21-year ride here. I walked in as a skinny 17-year-old in the back of Dale Thomas’ car with a surfboard that reeked out his whole car, and he was my Uber driver for four months. “I leave as a 38-year-old with a few grey hairs and a couple of premierships. I’m forever grateful to this football club so thank you.” There were sombre scenes in the rooms on Friday night as he hugged well-wishers minutes after leaving the field.

Advertisement

“It’s the next chapter of his journey. Collingwood have been unbelievable and have been super supportive to Scott around Scott’s decision,” Panozzo said. “But, at the same time, unfortunately things go their way last night, but at the same time he is really excited for him and his family and the kids for what’s next.” Magpies coach Craig McRae paid tribute to Pendlebury, who he said approached every day with humility, care and a willingness to learn. “We talk a lot about legacy in footy, but Scott’s legacy isn’t just the games or the records. It’s the impact he’s had on people,” he said in a club statement. Heading north: Pendlebury will not be in black and white in season 2027. Joe Armao “At Collingwood, we live in a state of growth mindset with no ceilings and he has led this from the front. He has been an incredible role model for his teammates and the wider club.”

Magpies president Barry Carp said Pendlebury would always be cherished by the club. “On behalf of everyone at Collingwood, I simply want to say thank you, Scott,” Carp said. “We’re enormously grateful for everything he’s given. Scott has represented Collingwood with class, dignity and excellence. It’s been a privilege for all of us to be part of his journey.” McRae said on Friday night he expected the Magpies to be aggressive through the trade and free agency period, as the club has considerable room in the salary cap. “I think we’re just in the business of getting better and at what level? I’m not sure, but we’ll be pushing hard. We put ourselves in a position to have a salary cap for the first time that’s got a healthy bank balance for want of a better term.

title: This common medication cuts heart-attack risk in older people
text:
Advertisement

NationalHealthcare This common medication cuts heart-attack risk in older people Henrietta Cook August 29, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Millions of older, healthy Australians could soon be advised to start taking statins after landmark research found the medication reduced the risk of heart attack and stroke by 30 per cent in those over 70. Until now, the benefits of taking the cholesterol-reducing drugs for otherwise healthy adults over 75 had been unclear. As a result, they had not been routinely prescribed as a preventative medicine for this cohort. Richard Milton has been taking statins following a heart attack in 2024. James Brickwood But a world-first clinical trial led by Monash University found the medication significantly reduced the risk of a major cardiovascular event in older adults who lived independently. The findings, which were published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday, also appear to dispel a persistent and false claim that statins cause dementia.

Advertisement

Co-author Dr Mark Nelson, a GP and adjunct professor at Monash University, said the findings would change the way doctors managed the risk of heart attack and stroke in older people. “It is really reassuring to see that you can continue to prescribe or initiate statins in the over 70s,” he said. “You have to make sure the benefit outweighs the harm, and that’s what we have demonstrated here.” Statins are the most commonly prescribed medications in Australia. Getty Images Statins are already one of the most commonly prescribed medications in Australia, with between 2.2 to 2.6 million people taking them daily.

Advertisement

They block the production of cholesterol in the liver. This lowers the amount circulating in a person’s blood, which can reduce and reverse cholesterol deposits in the arteries. Current Australian guidelines recommend statins for anyone with established heart disease. They are also prescribed as a preventative medicine for people aged 45 to 79 who are assessed as high risk using a cardiovascular disease risk calculator. But Professor Derek Chew, chief scientist and medical officer at the National Heart Foundation of Australia, said there had previously been a lack of robust evidence supporting the use of statins for people over 75. This is because older people had been historically overlooked in clinical trials of statins. He said this cohort were at increased risk of suffering a heart attack or stroke due to their age. While the public often assumes a heart attack leads to sudden death, Chew noted that most patients survive, often developing chronic conditions such as heart failure. Preventive therapies such as statins kept older adults out of hospitals and living independently, he said.

Advertisement

“For many people over the age of 70, it is about living well, not just about living longer. It’s about not being in hospital, not being debilitated by cardiovascular events. My patients always talk about wanting to live well.” Chew urged older Australians to discuss their five-year cardiovascular risk with their doctor. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Postcode lottery’: Royal Melbourne locks out suburban and regional patients The decade-long trial, known as The Statins in Reducing Events in the Elderly (STAREE), involved almost 10,000 participants who either took a statin or placebo. More than 3400 Australian GPs were involved in the trial. Older adults experienced the same cardiovascular benefits from statins – fewer heart attacks and strokes – as younger participants in previous trials.

Advertisement

In response to the landmark results, the National Heart Foundation of Australia is preparing to release updated clinical guidelines within the next six months to support GPs. Richard Milton was prescribed statins in December 2024 after he suffered a heart attack following a surfing competition on Sydney’s Northern Beaches. The fit and healthy 64-year-old recalled feeling strange and disassociated after the contest. The next minute, he had collapsed onto the bitumen of a nearby carpark and his friend was performing CPR on him. “It was a case of the right place, the right people,” Milton reflected. “Once the horse has bolted, it’s too late.” Milton was taken to hospital and later told that one of the arteries in his heart was completely blocked. A stent was placed in the blocked artery, and he has made a full recovery.

Advertisement

The now 66-year-old welcomes the findings into statins for older Australians, and said looming changes to clinical guidelines will save lives. He’s also pleased that the research has debunked the persistent claim that statins cause dementia, which was something he worried about before starting the medication. Related Article Opinion

Healthcare There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting Elly Goodsall Doctor The trial found no significant difference in dementia risk between the group who took a placebo and those who took statins. “It’s reassuring,” Milton said. “I have had no side effects, my memory hasn’t changed. I see no reason not to take them.”

Advertisement

Every year, an estimated 21,000 older Australians experience major cardiovascular events, such as heart attack and stroke. The risk of suffering these events increases with age. An estimated 60,000 Australians stopped or reduced their use of statins following a highly contentious two-part documentary aired on the ABC in 2013. The documentary by ABC’s Catalyst science show, questioned the link between elevated cholesterol and heart disease, suggesting that the benefits of statins were overstated and the drugs were overprescribed.
