title: More Australians are buying homes later. What does that mean for retirement?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Damian Hole's last mortgage repayment is due when he's 80.

The 52-year-old bought his first home about a decade ago and refinanced it in 2024, locking in a new 30-year loan term just before he turned 50.

He's among a growing cohort of Australians buying their first home later in life. People over the age of 40 accounted for nearly one in five first-home buyers last year (18.7 per cent), according to data from one of Australia's largest mortgage brokers, Aussie Home Loans.

That's up from just over 5.5 per cent in 2005.

At the other end, people under the age of 20 made up around a quarter of first-home buyers in 2005, compared with less than 0.5 per cent in 2025.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As housing affordability pressures make it harder for young Australians to enter the market, solutions designed to ease the path to home ownership have increasingly focused on expanding access to credit — allowing buyers to borrow more, with smaller deposits or longer mortgage terms.

Low-deposit loans can be accessed through the federal government's 5 per cent deposit scheme, while family guarantor loans allow first-time buyers to borrow up to 100 per cent of the purchase price.

A growing cohort of Australians are buying their first home later in life. Source: SBS News

Meanwhile, more lenders are offering 40-year mortgage terms, meaning some borrowers could be signing up to make repayments well into their later years.

If a growing number of Australians are buying homes later while taking on larger loans for longer, what happens when they reach retirement still saddled with mortgage debt?

'A cat and mouse game'

Making it easier for people to borrow can fuel higher house prices.

According to James Graham, a housing economics expert at the University of Sydney, without massively expanding housing supply, broadening access to credit alone is not a sustainable solution.

"It's just sort of a cat-and-mouse game," Graham tells SBS News.

"The prices go up, so we change mortgage credit. That pushes prices up further.

People are just borrowing more to buy more expensive houses, and they're not really any better off.

When the government introduced its 5 per cent deposit scheme last year, designed to help first-home buyers, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) predicted the measure would likely "put at least some further upward pressure" on housing price growth.

By March, the value of new loans taken out by first-home buyers was around 11 per cent higher than before the scheme was expanded in October, with the increase largely reflecting bigger average loan sizes, according to the RBA.

The costs of delayed home ownership

Graham says buying a first home later in life could have consequences beyond carrying mortgage debt into retirement. Entering the market at 40 or 50 leaves less time to build housing wealth and can reduce people's ability to move as their lives change.

"People are likely to be locked in for longer," he explains, warning that some buyers may end up remaining in homes that were intended as a first step into the market rather than a last stop.

"Less moving has its own social consequences," he adds.

"It means that people can't move back to communities that they wanted to be part of; they're further away from their children than they wanted to be; they're not near jobs that they want to be near.

"Maybe they've moved far out of the city because that's the only place they could buy. But now they're away from amenities and doctors."

Delayed home ownership and larger mortgages could also have implications for the aged care sector. Traditionally, many older Australians have relied on accessing housing equity (the portion of a property that is owned outright) to help fund retirement living or aged care, often through selling the family home. Unsettled mortgage debt could affect this transition, reducing the overall equity available.

Another concern is long-term mortgage stress, which can reduce the wellbeing of older Australians and may lead retirees to draw down their superannuation to pay off housing debt, according to 2019 research from the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI).

This, in turn, could place additional pressure on the pension system.

Currently, the Age Pension excludes the primary home from its assets test.

Paying down mortgage debt on a primary home with super can, therefore, reduce a person's assessable assets and potentially make them eligible for the pension.

"We have an ageing population in Australia, so the fiscal pressure on government will increase with that if government is supporting people through the pension system," AHURI managing director Tom Alves tells SBS News.

"The compulsory superannuation system is designed to address that issue, and if people are not having enough income through their super because they've used it to pay off their mortgage, obviously that's an issue."

AHURI's research notes that mortgage debt was uncommon among people aged 55-64 as early as the 1990s. Between 1996 and 2013, however, the proportion of Australians in that age bracket still paying off a mortgage rose from under 20 per cent to 45 per cent.

Home ownership has long underpinned Australia's retirement system, with policies, including the Age Pension, built on the assumption that most retirees own their home.

Widely used superannuation savings targets typically assume that people will own their homes outright by the time they reach retirement. While some modelling also considers renters, retirees still paying off a mortgage are largely left out of the picture.

"They do assume that people own their home," Susan Thorp, a retirement finance specialist at Monash University, tells SBS News.

"They're not allowing for the idea that someone may have, say, $150,000 of mortgage debt at the time they're retiring."

Yet a growing share of Australians may not fit those assumptions. In a January survey of 1,020 people by Loan Market Group, 58 per cent said they planned to own their home before retirement.

The rise of the 40-year mortgage

A small but growing number of Australian lenders have started offering 40-year mortgage terms, which can give borrowers access to loans they might not otherwise have been able to afford — but can add staggering extra interest costs over the life of the loan.

Source: SBS News

Richard Brown, a Mortgage Choice broker in the Sydney suburb of Epping, says many of his clients are eager to find ways to maximise their borrowing power, which is increasing their appetite for longer loan terms despite the downsides.

"There's an appetite for borrowers to get access to the money they need to buy the property they want," he says.

"They don't care what it is."

Sebastian Watkins, CEO and co-founder of mortgage broking giant Lendi Group, says relying on borrowing innovations like longer loan terms risks overlooking the underlying issue of unaffordable housing prices.

"We can't simply respond to people taking longer to save by giving them longer to pay off their loan," he tells SBS News.

If current trends continue, in a decade or two, Watkins expects the average Australian mortgage to be "larger, held later in life and managed much more dynamically".

We are likely to see longer loan terms, more family-supported or multi-generational borrowing and products that adapt as a customer's income, family circumstances and property needs change.

Japan offers an extreme historical example of intergenerational borrowing. Amid soaring housing costs in the 1980s, it experimented with 100-year mortgages designed to be repaid across multiple generations. Researchers who later modelled the loans concluded they did little to improve housing affordability.

What happens when debt stretches beyond careers?

Lenders assessing older applicants will typically look for a credible exit strategy demonstrating the loan can be comfortably managed in retirement, Watkins says.

"They may look at the expected loan balance at retirement age and consider the borrower's projected superannuation and other assets. Another potential strategy could be downsizing, where the borrower could sell the property and purchase a lower-value home," he says.

Hole, who bought his first home at 42, says his bank requested his superannuation balance before approving his mortgage.

"It was almost done, and then they requested my super balance, and then I realised, because my age will go beyond retirement, they're just seeing if I've got enough super to pay off the loan."

He says he should be able to comfortably repay the remainder of his mortgage with a lump sum from his super when he reaches retirement age, at which point he intends to access the Age Pension.

Damian Hole, 52, lives in Bacchus Marsh, Victoria, with his wife and three kids. Source: Supplied

The retirement debt challenge

Alves says there is no single policy fix, but governments need to consider both retirement and housing policy together.

Potential approaches include adjusting Age Pension settings to better reflect the differences between homeowners and non-homeowners, as well as expanding affordable housing options for older Australians, he says.

More broadly, he says improving access to home ownership earlier in life and increasing the supply of affordable rental housing could help reduce the number of Australians entering retirement with housing stress.

Thorp says there are fundamental questions that remain unanswered about what happens when more Australians enter retirement with housing debt.

"The question of how housing policy merges with superannuation and retirement policy is not fully worked out," she says.

title: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flood makes contact as disaster worsens
text:
Australian authorities are urgently trying to reach a woman who made contact with family after surviving catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) is engaging with local authorities on plans to assist the woman, who is understood to have been last reported in a remote area several days' hike from Kathmandu.

At least 38 Australians remain missing after an ice avalanche on Wednesday triggered Nepal's worst natural disaster in more than a decade.

Heavy continued rainfall is making rescue conditions difficult and unpredictable.

Further severe flooding, landslides and debris flows are predicted in the affected areas of Nepal and Tibet while a lake formed by the landslide has started to overflow.

Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was on a pilgrimage on the China-Nepal border when the catastrophic flash flooding hit.

Her husband Kailash Mansowar, who has not heard from her since, has travelled to the region from Sydney to find her, guided only by her iPhone's last location.

"Even the smallest piece of information could help bring her home," a widely shared post on social media announcing her disappearance reads.

A separate group of 15 Australians, including two boys aged 11 and 14, were travelling with US-based tourism operator Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Sydney doctor Manoj Dharmaratnam, who was invited to join the sacred pilgrimage but chose not to go, prescribed several of his friends altitude medication and conducted injury assessments before they left Australia.

"One of them had an injury and I did tell her, maybe you're not fit to go on this trek," Dr Dharmaratnam told AAP.

"She actually called up and cancelled her trip ... but then she said I've bought the ticket, so I might as well go."

The Himalayan Glacier group included a well-respected Sydney couple with two sons in their 20s, both studying medicine in NSW, he said.

READ MORE How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods

At least four Australians were travelling separately to tour groups, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday.

Wong said the federal government would send additional personnel to the region and unveiled a $5 million assistance package and humanitarian support.

An initial team of three humanitarian response specialists will be sent to help 20 staff already on the ground in Nepal.

But Chinese and Nepalese authorities say local rescue efforts could be complicated by further flooding, caused by a build-up of debris.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority on Thursday warned a lake was forming above the Rasuwagadhi border.

By Friday it had begun to overflow.

The Lhendi River had been obstructed about 18 kilometres above the border, posing a risk to residents in areas below, it said in a statement on social media.

The threat of a second flood caused by a blockage upstream led to evacuation orders at Jilong Port on the Nepal-China border, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

Rocks, boulders and debris lodged in the valley, as well as lakes forming along the plateau, could cause further flooding, geoscientist Jakob Steiner told AAP.

"Unfortunately it's not over ... this material is only going to lie there. We cannot move it away," Steiner, a fellow at the Asian Mountain Alliance, said.

"Every time a new flood comes, it's going to move this, and this is just going to increase future flood events in terms of impact."

title: How Australians can help those impacted by devastating Nepal floods
text:
IN BRIEF Donations will help provide emergency shelter, food, clean water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Australians can donate through the Emergency Action Alliance's Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal or by calling 1300 939 000.

Entire communities have been devastated by severe flooding and landslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, with homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure destroyed.

Search and rescue operations remain underway, while thousands of people are in urgent need of shelter, food, clean drinking water and medical assistance.

In response, 14 Australian charities have joined forces to launch a national appeal.

Emergency Action Alliance

The Emergency Action Alliance (EAA) has launched the Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal, bringing together a variety of charities to support communities affected by the disaster.

The alliance says donations will help provide immediate humanitarian assistance, including emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care.

Access to some affected communities remains difficult, with damaged roads and ongoing weather conditions hampering efforts to reach people in need.

Australians are encouraged to donate through the EAA website or by calling 1300 939 000.

The charities participating in the appeal are Save the Children Australia, Plan International Australia, Oxfam Australia, Australia for UNHCR, ActionAid Australia, CARE Australia, Caritas Australia, ADRA, Act for Peace, Anglican Overseas Aid, Australian Lutheran World Service, Baptist World Aid Australia, CBM Australia and Tearfund Australia.

EAA executive director Kerren Morris said the appeal provided Australians with a trusted way to support people affected by the disaster.

"Emergency shelter, food, safe drinking water and medical support are urgently needed now, while longer-term recovery efforts will continue for many months," she said in a statement.

What are the charities doing?

The charities involved bring different areas of humanitarian expertise to the response, with organisations and their local partners working to provide immediate assistance to affected communities.

Save the Children Australia

Save the Children is focusing on supporting children and families affected by humanitarian emergencies.

Oxfam Australia

Oxfam Australia's humanitarian work includes support for essential services such as clean water, sanitation and emergency assistance.

Australia for UNHCR

Australia for UNHCR is the UN refugee agency's national partner in Australia, and is supporting humanitarian assistance through the UNHCR network.

Homes and buildings have been left damaged and filled with debris after devastating flash floods swept through communities in Nepal. Source: Getty / Anadolu / Sunil Pradhan

What happens to donations?

The charities involved are continuing to assess the scale of the disaster and humanitarian needs in affected communities.

The EAA says its members are working to determine where support is most urgently needed as search and rescue operations continue.

The appeal has been endorsed by the Australian Council for International Development (ACFID), the peak body for Australian non-government organisations involved in humanitarian action and international development.

The ABC is also supporting the appeal through its ABC Gives initiative.

ACFID CEO Matthew Maury said coordinated action was critical as humanitarian needs continued to emerge.

"This appeal provides Australians with a trusted and effective way to support communities affected by this disaster," he said.

Australia pledges $5 million in aid

The Australian government has confirmed a $5 million humanitarian assistance package for communities affected by the devastating floods along the Nepal-China border.

The funding will support both the immediate disaster response and longer-term recovery, with the government saying it will help provide food, emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation.

The $5 million package will be delivered through established humanitarian partners, including $2 million to the World Food Programme for food and logistical support, $2 million through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership for emergency assistance including shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical care and psychosocial support, and $1 million to the EAA to support locally led recovery and rehabilitation efforts.

Assistant Foreign Affairs Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said Australian officials were working with Nepali authorities and tour operators to understand the situation and assess the needs of those affected.

Thistlethwaite also said the government was "working around the clock" to verify the status of Australians in the region, but damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure were making it difficult to establish contact.

More Australian support on the way

Australia will also deploy three humanitarian specialists to Nepal within 48 hours to help assess needs and support the emergency response.

The specialists are being deployed through the Australia Assists program and have expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning.

A crisis response team member and a regional consular officer are already on the ground in Kathmandu, alongside staff at the Australian embassy.

Australians in the affected region

Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the scale of the disaster and the remoteness of the affected region meant there were "immense challenges" ahead for the response and recovery.

"With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance," she said.

The government's humanitarian response comes as Australian officials continue to try to establish the whereabouts of Australians caught up in the disaster.

The latest government figure is at least 39 Australians reported missing.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is working with Nepali authorities, tour operators and others to verify their welfare and contact their families.

Australians requiring emergency consular assistance can contact the 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135 in Australia or +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas.

The government is also urging Australians in affected areas to follow the advice of local authorities and monitor official travel advice.

title: Questions were mounting at the border. Then they found a tunnel
text:
In brief A migrant tunnel between Belarus and Latvia has deepened a longstanding rift.

The tunnel's discovery has widened an already deep rift between the two countries.

Latvia's border guard has accused Belarusian authorities of partial responsibility for a recently discovered migrant tunnel beneath a border fence between the two nations.

The tunnel was uncovered by Latvian authorities in early August. Latvia faces an increasing number of migrants trying to cross the border from Belarus, further straining relations between the two countries.

Latvia shares a 173km border with Belarus. Latvia is a member of the European Union. Belarus, an independent nation with an authoritarian government, is not.

At the time of the tunnel's discovery, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said criminal networks were facilitating migration from Belarus into Latvia, bringing migrants into Europe's borderless Schengen area, but that the migrants' final destination was elsewhere on the continent.

"They migrate to where it's easier (to enter the EU). So we must not be the easiest place," Kulbergs told the press conference.

He pledged to target networks transporting the migrants from the border to their destinations, as well as any support points for migrants in Latvia, as part of what he called "Operation Werewolf".

"If everything goes according to plan, we are confident that we will already deal a serious enough blow to the system," Kulbergs said. "I want to tell the organisers: everything will be put to an end."

Latvia's government said in a statement it would cooperate with neighbours Estonia, Lithuania, Poland and others to stop the flow of migrants.

Latvia, along with Lithuania and Poland, has frequently accused Belarus' authoritarian government of smuggling migrants from crisis-impacted regions close to the EU's far borders.

The plot thickens

Having now discovered a second tunnel at another point along the border fence, Latvia is pointing fingers at the Belarusian border guard.

"It is simply impossible to build such a tunnel without the Belarusian border guards being aware of it," Guntis Pujats, head of the agency, told Latvian radio on Thursday.

Pujats went on to give more information about the original tunnel, saying that the entrance on the Belarusian side of the border was found around 10m from the border line and had been hidden among trees and bushes. The tunnel itself was reported to be 80cm wide and to run for roughly 30m.

Some 28 cubic metres of earth had been removed to construct the tunnel. Support structures had been erected within the tunnel to keep it from collapsing, and a plywood cover had been fitted to the entrance.

"The construction work was quite extensive. So the relevant authorities were undoubtedly aware of it," he said.

Pujats claimed that 12 underground tunnels have been found across Lithuania, along with the two found in Latvia to date.

The Belarusian government has not publicly commented on the existence of the tunnels.

title: France's cheese makers are confronting a problem tradition alone can't solve
text:
In brief A summer of record-breaking heatwaves and drought has taken a toll on France.

The unusually hot and dry conditions have started to affect France's beloved and protected cheesemakers.

Widespread drought and record-breaking heatwaves have forced France to relax some of its famously strict rules on cheese production, with authorities announcing special measures for abondance, beaufort and comte.

France's vast array of local cheeses are a source of national pride, and authorities go to great lengths to protect traditional production methods and ensure authenticity.

To earn a coveted "appellation d'origine protegee" (Protected Designation of Origin) label — and the right to give their cheese a particular protected name — producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.

But the summer's drought, which affected 95 per cent of mainland France in July, has left normally rich pastures dry and bare.

In response, the government said this week that producers of abondance, beaufort and comte, hard cheeses made from the raw milk of cows grazing in the Alps and Jura mountains, can supplement the animals' diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.

Growth on permanent grasslands as of 10 August is a third less than the 1989-2018 average, according to the agriculture ministry's statistical service.

The fodder situation is "highly degraded" in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.

The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules of origin, says it will also grant temporary relief for several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d'Auvergne, and fourme d'Ambert.

Europe's record-breaking summer heat has caused thousands of excess deaths, set wildfires blazing and seen major rivers drop to record lows.

In France, farmers are bracing for their smallest corn crop since 1980, and winegrowers are reporting some of the earliest harvests on record.

Scientists say human-caused climate change has intensified the drought, with extreme heat rather than low rainfall driving the dry conditions.

title: Nepal army races to save 100 people trapped in tunnel as flood death toll rises over 530
text:

Nepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue around 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by a devastating flood two days earlier.

title: This Australian crisis is entering a 'confronting' new phase
text:
IN BRIEF More than 2,500 Australians died from drug-induced overdose in 2024, the highest on record.

Older Australians accounted for almost half of reported deaths.

This article contains references to substance abuse and suicide.

Drug-induced deaths have hit a record high, with older Australians accounting for more than half of the fatalities.

Australia's Annual Overdose Report, released by the Penington Institute, documented 2,596 drug-induced deaths in 2024, with 80.5 per cent being from unintentional overdose.

Since 2008, more Australians have died from drug-induced deaths than road fatalities — with an average of 31 years lost per death.

"The data is quite confronting," Jake Dizard, director of research at the Penington Institute, told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The report found that the median age of people dying from drug overdose is increasing.

For the first time, those aged between 50 and 59 accounted for almost half of all unintentional overdose deaths.

Dizard said it could be attributed to "an ageing large cohort of people who started using drugs in the 1990s and early 2000s".

"As that cohort has got older, they have become more vulnerable to drug-induced death because of the length of time that they have been using drugs and the accumulating sort of comorbidities," he said.

The report also noted that of the 428 drug-induced suicides, 39 per cent were people aged 60 and over.

Australian Alcohol and Other Drugs Council CEO Melanie Walker said the report confirms that overdose is not a "young people problem".

"Overdose is something that affects the whole community," she told SBS News.

"It affects young people. It also affects older people. Overdose can be from illicit drug use, or it can be from prescription drug use."

The report also found that men accounted for 72.7 per cent of unintentional drug-induced deaths, people living in regional and rural areas had higher rates of death than those living in capital cities, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced higher rates of overdose.

In 2024, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people experienced an overdose rate of 29.3 per 100,000 compared to 6.6 per 100,000 for non-Indigenous people.

Opioids were responsible for 42 per cent of all drug-induced deaths in 2024, with heroin-related deaths rising from 101 deaths in 2001 to 488 deaths in 2024.

Amphetamines were involved in 772 deaths, a record high for the drug, and cocaine was involved in 141 deaths. Benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants also contributed to drug-induced deaths.

Dizard said that the use of prescription opioids, such as oxycodone, has declined since 2021 — a trend seen across "a number of categories of prescription drugs".

Cocaine was the only recorded drug that saw a decrease in the median age of people dying from overdose.

Two-thirds of Australians turned away from services

The majority of drug-induced deaths in Australia are preventable, Dizard said.

The report listed a range of recommendations to reduce the number of deaths, including increased access to the medicine naloxone.

"It's an opioid overdose reversal drug, which is very safe and can be administered by anybody," Dizard said.

"It's important not just for people who habitually or routinely use opioids, but also people who might be using other drugs, including cocaine, that might be contaminated with some sort of opioid."

Dizard noted the importance of community education on how to identify signs of overdose and respond — and greater investment in services, specifically opioid pharmacotherapy.

While stigma hinders people's ability to seek support for drug and alcohol addiction, Dizard said a major issue is a lack of funding for services.

He said law enforcement is heavily funded, and a "more balanced approach to drug policy" is needed.

"Funding has been incredibly unbalanced throughout the last several decades of Australian drug policy."

Australia's National Drug Strategy has three pillars: supply reduction, which includes law enforcement; demand reduction, which refers to treatment; and harm reduction, including preventative measures such as drug checks.

"The supply reduction pillar has traditionally had double the funding of treatment," Walker said.

She said that more than two-thirds of people seeking help for drug and alcohol use have been turned away from services because of funding insufficiency.

Walker said there's currently no forum for governments, both federal and state and territory, to come together and "talk about the implementation of the national drug strategy and do coordinated planning".

"For at least the last 10 years, half a million Australians have been missing out on getting to alcohol and other drug treatment because there's simply no place for them," she said.

"It's really obvious what the problem is in terms of why overdose deaths are rising, and until we come to terms with that and get proper resources — I can't see that changing."

SBS News has contacted the Department of Health for comment.

title: 'Creative thinking is born of loneliness': Artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
text:
In brief Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama died in hospital in Tokyo earlier this month.

The artist was famous for her enigmatic polka dot designs.

The dotty pumpkins and kaleidoscope rooms of Yayoi Kusama, who has died aged 97, were as vibrant as the artist herself, but her exuberant work was the expression of a long battle with mental illness.

Once a fixture of the 1960s pop and minimalist scenes in New York, Japan's "polka dot queen" found huge commercial success in her later decades.

Her larger-than-life paintings, sculptures and installations — inspired by vivid hallucinations — sold for millions of dollars and packed out top galleries.

Kusama, instantly recognisable in her bright red wig and bold spotted outfits, worked well into old age from the psychiatric hospital in Tokyo where she lived voluntarily for the second half of her life.

But she also struggled with her feelings for her home country, which she left for decades and once described as "full of disdain for women".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Born in 1929, the youngest daughter of a wealthy but troubled family, Kusama started producing her signature dot and net patterns at the age of 10.

"My mother had regrets about my birth, and I was driven to the edge psychologically," she wrote in her autobiography, A Personal History of Polka Dots.

"One day, after seeing a tablecloth with a red flower pattern on a desk, I saw the same red flower pattern all over the ceiling, windows and pillars. It filled the room, and covered my body."

Art provided a release for the young Kusama, whose father, a seedling merchant, was unfaithful to her mother.

"When I was sad or lonely, everything would be cured when I drew pictures," she said.

In the book, Kusama explained her concept of "self-obliteration" — a recurrent theme throughout her career.

"I put dots all over my body and make all the surroundings dot patterns. By creating the same thing over and over, my own existence is buried in the art."

60s 'happenings'

Kusama studied Japanese painting in Kyoto, against her parents' wishes, and held her first solo exhibition in 1952 in her hometown of Matsumoto in central Japan.

At the show, she met a psychiatrist who advised her to go and work abroad — an idea that appealed to her.

"Japan was so small, vulgar, feudalistic and full of disdain for women," said the artist.

"I was born and raised in Japan, but I'm not influenced by Japanese culture and tradition."

The decisive push to pack her bags came when she wrote to modernist painter Georgia O'Keeffe, who encouraged Kusama to seek international recognition in the United States.

Yayoi Kusama's installation "Infinity Mirrored Room— The Hope of the Polka Dots Buried in Infinity Will Eternally Cover the Universe". Source: AFP / Ina Fassbender

Kusama moved to Seattle in 1957 and then to New York, where she struggled to find her place as an Asian artist in the city's largely white, male-dominated creative scene.

"I was at the lowest point of poverty. One time, I couldn't eat for three days because I had no money," she once told Japan's Asahi Shimbun newspaper.

"I even ate the breadcrumbs left by the pigeons."

But she persevered and, during her 16 years in New York, became a prominent figure in the avant-garde world.

At the height of the 1960s sexual liberation movement, she would stage "happenings", where people stripped naked on Wall Street or in Central Park and had their bodies painted with polka dots.

In 2024, Yayoi Kusama's iconic dots wrapped 60 plane trees in Melbourne. Source: AFP / William West

She also launched a fashion line, established a "Church of Self-Obliteration" and styled herself the "High Priestess of Polka Dots" to officiate at a gay wedding.

Global fame

By the time she returned to Japan in 1973, Kusama was burned out, and checked herself into a psychiatric ward where she lived for the rest of her life.

And it was not until the 1990s that her vivid patterns, bold floral shapes and shiny steel orbs hit the mainstream, later providing the backdrop to countless selfies.

Pumpkins are her most famous motif, featuring heavily in her paintings and giant sculptures.

The artist called them her "life partners", saying she had first grown to love their "generous, unpretentious looks" as a child.

Kusama was named the world's most popular artist in 2014 by The Art Newspaper.

She was also one of the most expensive, with one of her "infinity net" paintings fetching nearly US$8 million ($11 million) at a 2019 auction.

But fame and fortune did not affect her remarkable originality, which she once attributed to the "serenity of the soul" that comes from spending time alone.

"Creative thinking is born of loneliness ... because I stood before the art all alone, I was able to forge my own path," Kusama said.

She published several novels in her later years, while her exhibitions continued to draw huge crowds.

"My wish after my death is that the eternally bright future, the beauty of human love and my soul will be passed on," Kusama told reporters in 2017.

"Please love my artwork, even after I die."

Kusama died on 14 August in Tokyo.

title: This common medication cuts heart-attack risk in older people
text:

Millions of older, healthy Australians could soon be advised to start taking statins after landmark research found the medication reduced the risk of heart attack and stroke by 30 per cent in those over 70. Until now, the benefits of taking the cholesterol-reducing drugs for otherwise healthy adults over 75 had been unclear. As a result, they had not been routinely prescribed as a preventative medicine for this cohort. Richard Milton has been taking statins following a heart attack in 2024. James Brickwood But a world-first clinical trial led by Monash University found the medication significantly reduced the risk of a major cardiovascular event in older adults who lived independently. The findings, which were published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday, also appear to dispel a persistent and false claim that statins cause dementia.

Advertisement

Co-author Dr Mark Nelson, a GP and adjunct professor at Monash University, said the findings would change the way doctors managed the risk of heart attack and stroke in older people. “It is really reassuring to see that you can continue to prescribe or initiate statins in the over 70s,” he said. “You have to make sure the benefit outweighs the harm, and that’s what we have demonstrated here.” Statins are the most commonly prescribed medications in Australia. Getty Images Statins are already one of the most commonly prescribed medications in Australia, with between 2.2 to 2.6 million people taking them daily.

Advertisement

They block the production of cholesterol in the liver. This lowers the amount circulating in a person’s blood, which can reduce and reverse cholesterol deposits in the arteries. Current Australian guidelines recommend statins for anyone with established heart disease. They are also prescribed as a preventative medicine for people aged 45 to 79 who are assessed as high risk using a cardiovascular disease risk calculator. But Professor Derek Chew, chief scientist and medical officer at the National Heart Foundation of Australia, said there had previously been a lack of robust evidence supporting the use of statins for people over 75. This is because older people had been historically overlooked in clinical trials of statins. He said this cohort were at increased risk of suffering a heart attack or stroke due to their age. While the public often assumes a heart attack leads to sudden death, Chew noted that most patients survive, often developing chronic conditions such as heart failure. Preventive therapies such as statins kept older adults out of hospitals and living independently, he said.

Advertisement

“For many people over the age of 70, it is about living well, not just about living longer. It’s about not being in hospital, not being debilitated by cardiovascular events. My patients always talk about wanting to live well.” Chew urged older Australians to discuss their five-year cardiovascular risk with their doctor. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Postcode lottery’: Royal Melbourne locks out suburban and regional patients The decade-long trial, known as The Statins in Reducing Events in the Elderly (STAREE), involved almost 10,000 participants who either took a statin or placebo. More than 3400 Australian GPs were involved in the trial. Older adults experienced the same cardiovascular benefits from statins – fewer heart attacks and strokes – as younger participants in previous trials.

Advertisement

In response to the landmark results, the National Heart Foundation of Australia is preparing to release updated clinical guidelines within the next six months to support GPs. Richard Milton was prescribed statins in December 2024 after he suffered a heart attack following a surfing competition on Sydney’s Northern Beaches. The fit and healthy 64-year-old recalled feeling strange and disassociated after the contest. The next minute, he had collapsed onto the bitumen of a nearby carpark and his friend was performing CPR on him. “It was a case of the right place, the right people,” Milton reflected. “Once the horse has bolted, it’s too late.” Milton was taken to hospital and later told that one of the arteries in his heart was completely blocked. A stent was placed in the blocked artery, and he has made a full recovery.

Advertisement

The now 66-year-old welcomes the findings into statins for older Australians, and said looming changes to clinical guidelines will save lives. He’s also pleased that the research has debunked the persistent claim that statins cause dementia, which was something he worried about before starting the medication. Related Article Opinion

Healthcare There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting Elly Goodsall Doctor The trial found no significant difference in dementia risk between the group who took a placebo and those who took statins. “It’s reassuring,” Milton said. “I have had no side effects, my memory hasn’t changed. I see no reason not to take them.”

Advertisement

Every year, an estimated 21,000 older Australians experience major cardiovascular events, such as heart attack and stroke. The risk of suffering these events increases with age. An estimated 60,000 Australians stopped or reduced their use of statins following a highly contentious two-part documentary aired on the ABC in 2013. The documentary by ABC’s Catalyst science show, questioned the link between elevated cholesterol and heart disease, suggesting that the benefits of statins were overstated and the drugs were overprescribed. title: 616 now dead, sad twist in hunt for Aussies
text:
A missing Australian man from the NSW South Coast had reached the Nepal-Tibet border just 10 minutes before flash flooding hit the region, as the death toll continues to climb.

616 people have died in the natural disaster, and the total number of those unaccounted for spiked to 2400 overnight, with 41 Australians among them.

Michael Keats has been confirmed as one of the missing 41 and had just reached the Nepal-Tibet border just moments before disaster struck, his family revealed in a statement.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Keats' relatives first thought he was safe, however, quickly learned he was unaccounted for.

"Confusion around the timing of the floods initially led us to believe our beautiful Michael would be safe in Kathmandu, preparing to fly home," they said in a statement.

Michael Keats, from the South Coast in New South Wales, is one of the 41 Australians reported missing after the floods in Nepal. Picture: Supplied

"Unfortunately, it was confirmed relatively quickly by the Isha Foundation that Michael and his Kailash travel group had arrived at Gyirong Port on the Nepal-Tibet border just 10 minutes before the tragic floods hit."

Mr Keats' family said their thoughts and prayers are with every person affected by this tragic event.

"We are praying for a miracle for our beautiful Michael. Michael is the most beautiful soul," they said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"He is gentle and kind, with a unique light that touches everyone lucky enough to know him."

His sister, Karen Hayley, said Mr Keats was "a seeker, an adventurer, a truly beautiful soul." "He travelled to this sacred part of the world on a journey that held such deep meaning for him," she told followers on social media.

"He is currently missing in Nepal and while our hearts are carrying the unbearable weight of not knowing, we are holding onto hope and praying for a miracle.

"Come home to us, Mike. You are loved beyond words."

In a separate post she revealed her family had gathered at his "happy place", in Sydney's south. A photo showed the family had created a vigil with photos of Mr Keats and candles, and gathered around.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"This is the most surreal experience of my life," she wrote in a third post.

"Michael is missing, not confirmed deceased yet the grief is already immeasurable. There is still hope and we are holding on to that with everything we have. But at the same time, my heart is trying to comprehend something it simply cannot."

Meanwhile, Karan Bhardwaj, 40, a Brisbane father and member of the Royal Australian Air Force has been identified as another one of the Australians currently missing in Nepal.

He was travelling with tour operator Kailash Journeys when the disaster hit on Wednesday morning.

"We're desperately waiting for news and praying with everything we have that Karan is safe and will come home to us all," his sister Jen Nai told the ABC.

Karan Bhardwaj is a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force missing in Nepal.

Satellite image shows part of the town of Timure, Nepal on July 1, 2026, before the flash flooding. (Photo by Satellite image Â©2026 Vantor / AFP)

Satellite image shows part of the town of Timure, Nepal on August 28, 2026, after the flash flooding. (Photo by Satellite image Â©2026 Vantor / AFP)

Assistant Foreign Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said Australian DFAT officials are "working around the clock" and getting as close to the region as they possibly can.

Advertisement Advertisement

"Yesterday, Foreign minister, Penny Wong, had a phone call with the Nepalese Foreign Minister to express our deepest sympathies to the people of Nepal and to offer Australia's support," he said.

"As a result, we've announced $5m worth of humanitarian aid to support the rescue and recovery and provide vital supplies to the affected communities and to ensure that Australia is doing its bit to help out.

"We've also been in touch with members of the Nepalese community here in Australia."

Minister Thistlethwaite said he attended a vigil at Strathfield on Friday night in unity with the Nepalese community to offer his support.

"Our condolences and to do all we can to get them through this difficult period," he said.

Earlier on Saturday morning Minister Thistlethwaite said the government was working with crews from the Department of Foreign Affairs to "try and make contact with as many Australians as possible that we know are missing", as well as family members who had flown in to help with the search.

"We are working with people who are in the region, the Australians that we know," he told ABC Breakfast.

"The roads are cut off. About 50,000 homes have been destroyed. There is no telecommunications infrastructure to the region. Power has been cut off.

"So, our DFAT officials are getting as close as they possibly can to the region and we're working with those Australians that we know are on the ground there, trying to locate their loved ones, to provide them with as much support as possible."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Late on Friday, the family of a Melbourne woman shared one of the few pieces of good news out of the region; their daughter was safe, had managed to find a phone and would be trekking for multiple days back to Kathmandu.

NSW Premier Chris Minns said on Saturday that he is joining the chorus of concern for those caught up in the disaster.

"Literally hundreds of people have lost their lives, potentially thousands. I know that there are many who are still missing, including Australians right now," he said on Saturday.

"Our heart bleeds for them. I imagine their families back in Australia are incredibly worried, and as the days go on, and the prospects of mining have become more and more dim, that anxiety can get worse and worse.

"I want them to know that the people of NSW and Australia are with them."

Emergency teams have recovered 584 bodies as they work through the disaster area, and Nepal's disaster authority has added 933 hydropower workers to the list of the missing in Nepal and China, bringing the figure to 2400.

Many of the Australians in the region were on religious pilgrimages. The Nepal Tourism Board has been providing numbers of citizens of various countries who have been rescued; Indians, South Koreans, Chinese, Russians, Americans, Italians and a Bulgarian citizen have been saved.

As of late on Friday, no Australians had appeared on the salvation list.

A family friend of the NSW family, Chin Valsan, said Ms Patel was about to finish her pilgrimage when the disaster struck on Wednesday, and she had not been heard from since.

Bhavin Patel flew NSW on Friday morning.

"He's putting up a brave face for his kids but on the inside, he must be so distressed," their friend told the ABC.

Ms Patel was one of 11 Australians trekking to Mount Kailash and checked in with immigration at the Tibet-Nepal border very shortly before the area was flooded.

Many of the most-damaged areas are now only accessible by helicopter.

But on Friday rescue efforts in one area were stopped for 90 minutes as a lake, created by the falling chunk of glacier which started the disaster, burst its banks.

'Running for their life'

Sharmina da Manandhar from UNICEF told the ABC the scale of the recovery efforts is "seismic" and international help is urgently needed.

"We are working very closely with the people of Nepal and doing everything we can to ensure children are protected, they have safe, they have safe water, they have the basic supplies, like hygiene materials that they require, so we are doing everything we can," she said on Saturday morning.

However, Ms Manandhar said their concerns about ongoing risks of further flooding remain high.

"Yes, we are aware of the risk, and we have heard reports regarding this, so this just highlights the need to reach at effected children and families as soon as possible," she said.

"They require the support and we need to reach them as soon as possible."

Ms Manandhar described the situation as dire, and said dozens of people including women and children were sheltering inside one small school.

"They are staying there. They don't have anything. Imagine having to run for your life and you don't have a moment to pick up anything that you require," she said.

"They were just running for their life. They only have the clothes on their back, they don't have anything.

Recovery efforts are underway as families begin rebuilding and restoring daily life. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

Flood-affected communities in Rasuwa are facing significant damage to homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Picture: NewsWire Handout/ World Vision

"There are women who are on their periods and young girls there saying they don't have the hygiene supplies, so UNICEF yesterday dispatched hygiene kits.

"The basic things of health care, have been wash add way. Schoolchildren have washed school supplies, pencils book, everything they had – everything has gone."

More to come

title: Vibe strong for by-election win, says One Nation
text:
One Nation looks poised for a by-election victory in the west, as Labor bemoans a toxic campaign invaded by "poisonous" east coast trolls.

Voters in the safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour are casting ballots after senior minister Paul Papalia's mid-term retirement triggered the contest.

Pauline Hanson's One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen has been buoyed by a sea of polling booth orange across the beachside state electorate, south of Perth.

Long held by Labor, is Secret Harbour poised to fall to One Nation's Luke Herdegen? (Richard Wainwright/AAP PHOTOS)

"The vibe has been really strong for the last six weeks," he told AAP late Saturday morning.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We're feeling confident but ... it's a big margin. The swing is definitely on but it's just a matter of how big."

WA Premier Roger Cook wasn't throwing in the towel but conceded it would be a battle to hold the outer-suburban mortgage-belt electorate despite Labor's 11.5 per cent margin.

"It would break my heart," he said when asked about defeat.

"By-elections bring up all kinds of opportunities for a whole range of issues to impact on the seat."

Premier Roger Cook acknowledges that victory presents as an uphill battle. (Richard Wainwright/AAP PHOTOS)

On the ground in Secret Harbour, Labor is on the nose, with cost-of-living pressures, housing and a perceived lack of community amenities topping lists of voter concerns.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Local Luke Pors voted for One Nation and believes it will do a better job than either Labor or Liberal.

"We know what their true goal is and I think just in One Nation we trust," he said.

The Qantas flight attendant was also impressed by Mr Herdegen's campaign.

"He's like a home buddy and as obviously a youngie; we can really connect with him," he said.

Flight attendant Luke Pors says he's placed his trust in One Nation. (Aaron Bunch/AAP PHOTOS)

Retirees Ann and Les Scard also voted One Nation.

"It has been a pretty strong campaign by Luke Herdegen," Mr Scard said.

"He deserves a chance.

"I get the impression Liberal and Labor are desperate; they're doing everything to try and discredit them and I don't think they're being successful."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mrs Scard isn't concerned by One Nation's controversial immigration policy.

"I agree with a lot of what Pauline Hanson says," she said.

"Something has to be done, it's just all askew."

One Nation's polling booth presence has been strong. (Richard Wainwright/AAP PHOTOS)

Mr Herdegen believes people are desperate for change

"They're struggling with cost of living; there's a major housing issue here with the mass immigration coming through and people have just had enough," he said.

Retired truck driver Dean Maxwell isn't so sure. He voted Labor.

"I didn't vote for One Nation, I put them last," he said.

"I just don't see any good policy.

"I don't like any of the pollies but I particularly don't like Pauline Hanson.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I think she's in Gina Rinehart's pocket."

Retired truckie Dean Maxwell put One Nation last. (Aaron Bunch/AAP PHOTOS)

Labor candidate Georgia Tree said she would fight until the polls closed but admitted protest votes against the status quo could hurt her prospects.

"It's been an absolute roller coaster," she said.

"I have my eyes completely open to that and it will be very interesting to see once the counting's done.

"It's always tough in a by-election. We've seen right-wing populism take place all over the globe and Australia is not immune."

One Nation's performance in the tradie-haven will be of interest across the nation, particularly Victoria, which has a state election in November.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It could have longer-term implications for senior federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, whose marginal seat of Canning takes in Secret Harbour and is being openly targeted by One Nation.

Georgia Tree concedes protest votes against could hurt her prospects. (Richard Wainwright/AAP PHOTOS)

Mr Cook lamented One Nation's involvement in a fierce campaign that saw police deployed at some polling places.

"We have the full brunt of One Nation nationally focused on this electorate," he said.

"We've all seen some of the incredibly toxic and poisonous social media activity coming from bots and trolls, both on the east coast and overseas."

WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies rejected the assertion and accused Labor of the same behaviour.

"They're going to try to blame anything on their loss," he said.
